title: Question 5

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Use Fig. 5.1 to determine the frequency of wave $X$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 5.1 and find the time for one complete oscillation - for example from one peak at 0 ms to the next peak.
Hint 2: Convert that period from ms to s, then think how frequency is linked to period by a reciprocal relationship.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the period from the graph**
You are looking at how displacement at a fixed point changes with time. One full cycle means the motion repeats exactly. In Fig. 5.1 the wave starts at a peak $y = 2.0 \text{ cm}$ at $t = 0$ and next reaches the same peak at $t = 4.0 \text{ ms}$. So $$T = 4.0 \text{ ms} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Convert period to frequency**
Frequency is the number of oscillations per second: $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$ Put the period in seconds first: $$f = \frac{1}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 250 \text{ Hz}$$

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A second wave $Z$ with the same frequency as wave $X$ also passes point $P$. Wave $Z$ has intensity $2I$. The phase difference between the two waves is $90^{\circ}$.

On Fig. 5.1, sketch the variation with time $t$ of the displacement $y$ of wave $Z$.

Show your working.

markscheme_points.text: curve with same period and with amplitude $2.8 \text{cm}$
curve shifted $1.0 \text{ms}$ to left or to right of wave X

hints: Hint 1: Start with intensity - recall how intensity depends on amplitude, and use the peak of wave X at 2.0 cm to work out the new peak for intensity 2I.
Hint 2: Since wave Z has the same frequency as X, think what that tells you about its period and shape on the same time axis.
Hint 3: A 90 degree phase difference is a quarter of a full 360 degree cycle - think what fraction of the 4.0 ms period that corresponds to as a sideways shift.
parts.proper_answer: Amplitude of Z $= 2.0\sqrt{2} = 2.8 \text{ cm}$. Same period $4.0 \text{ ms}$, sinusoidal curve shifted by $1.0 \text{ ms}$ left or right relative to X.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the new amplitude from intensity**
Intensity of a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude: $$I \propto A^2$$ So if intensity doubles from $I$ to $2I$: $$\frac{A_Z}{A_X} = \sqrt{2}$$ Wave X has $A_X = 2.0 \text{ cm}$, so $$A_Z = 2.0 \times \sqrt{2} \approx 2.8 \text{ cm}$$ That is the peak height your sketched curve must reach.

Step 2: **Keep the same period**
Same frequency means same period. So wave Z must also repeat every $4.0 \text{ ms}$. Draw a sine-type wave with exactly the same wavelength along the time axis as wave X, but taller at $2.8 \text{ cm}$.

Step 3: **Apply the 90 degree phase shift**
A full cycle is $360^{\circ}$ or one period $4.0 \text{ ms}$. So $90^{\circ}$ is one quarter of a cycle: $$\Delta t = \frac{90}{360} \times T = \frac{T}{4} = 1.0 \text{ ms}$$ Shift the whole Z curve $1.0 \text{ ms}$ to the left or to the right of X. For example, where X has a peak at 0 ms, Z passes through zero.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Use the gradient of the line in Fig. 5.3 to determine the wavelength, in nm, of the laser light.
hints: Hint 1: Recall the double-slit equation linking fringe width $x$, wavelength $\lambda$, slit separation $a$ and screen distance $D$.
Hint 2: Compare that equation with $y = mx + c$ for the $x$ against $D$ graph to see what the gradient represents.
Hint 3: Pick two widely spaced points on the line in Fig. 5.3 to calculate gradient $\Delta x / \Delta D$, taking care to convert $x$ from mm to m.
Hint 4: Multiply your gradient by the slit separation $a = 0.45 \text{ mm}$ in metres to get $\lambda$, then convert to nm.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link gradient to wavelength**
For double-slit interference: $$x = \frac{\lambda D}{a}$$ So a plot of $x$ against $D$ is a straight line through the origin in theory, with: $$\text{gradient} = \frac{\lambda}{a}$$ Hence $$\lambda = \text{gradient} \times a$$ Here $a = 0.45 \text{ mm} = 0.45 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Calculate the gradient from Fig. 5.3**
Choose a large triangle for accuracy, e.g. $x = 2.4 \text{ mm}$ at $D = 1.75 \text{ m}$ to $x = 4.5 \text{ mm}$ at $D = 3.25 \text{ m}$: $$\text{gradient} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta D} = \frac{(4.5-2.4)\times 10^{-3}}{3.25-1.75}$$ $$\text{gradient} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-3}$$ Note the $10^{-3}$ because $x$ is in mm.

Step 3: **Find wavelength and convert to nm**
$$\lambda = 1.4 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.45 \times 10^{-3}$$ $$\lambda \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$$ Since $1 \text{ nm} = 10^{-9} \text{ m}$: $$\lambda \approx 630 \text{ nm}$$ This is red light, sensible for this type of laser.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: The separation of the slits is increased. State and explain the effects, if any, on the graph of Fig. 5.3.

markscheme_points.text: (gradient is equal to $\lambda / a$ therefore) gradient of line is reduced
value of $x$ will be reduced for all values of $D$ or new line is completely below old line or intercept is less

hints: Hint 1: Think again about what the gradient of the $x$ against $D$ line equals in terms of $\lambda$ and $a$, and what happens to that fraction if $a$ gets larger.
Hint 2: If the gradient gets smaller, think what that means for the value of $x$ at any given $D$ and where the new line sits compared with the old one.
parts.proper_answer: Gradient $= \lambda/a$ decreases so fringe width $x$ is smaller for each $D$. New line has smaller gradient and lies completely below the old line.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why gradient falls**
From $x = \lambda D / a$, gradient $= \lambda / a$. Wavelength $\lambda$ is unchanged but slit separation $a$ is increased, so the fraction $\lambda / a$ gets smaller. The line becomes less steep.

Step 2: **Describe the new line**
For any fixed $D$, $x$ is proportional to $1/a$, so $x$ is reduced. The new straight line therefore lies entirely below the original line in Fig. 5.3.
